definition: Verbose means using far more words than the message needs — wordy to the point that the extra words bury the point.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word verbose. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know verbose should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandpa's voicemails are verbose: a full minute of weather, knee updates, and a review of lunch before the actual question finally arrives.
Wordy is the mild, everyday rung below verbose — a few more words than needed; verbose goes further, with padding heavy enough to start burying the point.
Prolix, this unit's own heavyweight, is stronger than verbose: verbose writing wastes words along the way, while prolix talk overruns its point so far that the listener loses the thread entirely.

Long-winded is the everyday complaint about talk that goes on far too long, usually tediously. Verbose is the more clinical charge, and it points at the words themselves: too many of them for the content, whether on the page or out loud.

Rambling faults the direction — talk that drifts from topic to topic with no plan or thread, and a rambling toast can be over in a minute. Verbose is strictly a charge about word count: more words than the message needs, however tidily they are organized.

Verbose means using far more words than the message needs — wordy to the point that the extra words bury the point.
The new hire's status emails were so verbose — every meeting recapped, every hallway chat footnoted — that her manager began skimming them for verbs.
When she trimmed one down to its four real updates, replies came back within minutes.

Verbose is a charge about quantity: the emails' information was fine — four updates — but it arrived wrapped in ten times the words it needed, and that padding, not the ideas underneath it, is what verbose condemns.
Verbose is the plainest of this unit's charges against overwriting: it simply counts.
Prolix adds tedium and a lost thread; turgid, the unit's adjective for swollen prose, adds self-importance; grandiloquence adds pomp.
Verbose just says there are too many words for the content — which is why editors reach for it first.

When Priya became treasurer, the hiking club handed her its bylaws: forty-one pages for a group that owns two tents.
The rules themselves were sensible and the layout orderly.
The writing was verbose: no sentence used ten words where thirty could be made to fit.
Article Nine, on returning borrowed gear, took three paragraphs to say 'bring it back clean within a week.' Priya's rewrite changed no rule.
She only cut words -- whole clauses of throat-clearing vanished, openings that apologized for beginning -- and the same bylaws now run six pages.
At the vote to adopt them, a founding member sighed with relief: 'So that's what our rules say.'
